bib.title: Chapter 1. Exploratory Data Analysis (Practical Statistics for Data Scientists)

question: What are the basic summaries and plots for a first look at data in a data science project?
contributions: Defines data types, rectangular data, estimates of location and variability, distribution plots, categorical summaries, correlation and multivariate exploration, with R code.

limits: Code is R only; formulas are images and absent from the text.
The chapter prints no author names; the Bruce & Bruce attribution comes from the note's citation.
Dataset sizes not stated for most examples (state data is 50 states, inferred).
Rank-based correlations (Spearman, Kendall) are only mentioned.
practices: Treat the first step of any data project as looking at the data, by summarising and visualising it (Summary).
Use median, trimmed mean or weighted estimates when outliers or unequal groups distort the mean (Median and Robust Estimates).
Trim 10% from each end as a common robust choice (Median and Robust Estimates).
Use MAD, IQR or percentiles instead of SD when outliers are present (Estimates of Variability).
Include empty bins in frequency tables and try different bin sizes (Frequency Table and Histograms).
Use hexagonal binning or contours instead of scatterplots for hundreds of thousands of records (Hexagonal Binning).
Use contingency tables for two categorical variables and boxplots or violin plots for numeric versus categorical (Two Categorical Variables).
Condition on a third variable with facets to explain clusters (Visualizing Multiple Variables).
Stay with Pearson correlation and robust variants for exploration; Pearson fails for nonlinear association and is outlier-sensitive (Correlation).
Prefer bar charts to pie charts (Exploring Binary and Categorical Data).
Declare categorical types explicitly, but beware read.csv auto-converting text to factors that turn new values into NA (Elements of Structured Data).

terms.definition: The sum of all values divided by the number of values.
The sum of all values times a weight divided by the sum of the weights.
The value such that one-half of the data lies above and below.
The average of all values after dropping a fixed number of extreme values.
A data value that is very different from most of the data.
The sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by n – 1 where n is the number of data values.
The square root of the variance.
The mean of the absolute value of the deviations from the mean.

terms.term: Median absolute deviation from the median
terms.definition: The median of the absolute value of the deviations from the median.
The value such that P percent of the values take on this value or less and (100–P) percent take on this value or more.
The difference between the 75th percentile and the 25th percentile.
A tally of the count of numeric data values that fall into a set of intervals (bins).
A smoothed version of the histogram, often based on a kernal density estimate.
When the categories can be associated with a numeric value, this gives an average value based on a category’s probability of occurrence.
A metric that measures the extent to which numeric variables are associated with one another (ranges from –1 to +1).
A tally of counts between two or more categorical variables.
A plot of two numeric variables with the records binned into hexagons.
Similar to a boxplot but showing the density estimate.
